title: Why Central Banks Are Always Late to the Party
abstract: Central banks keep showing up after the music stops, and I'm tired of pretending that's a strategy.
body:
## The eternal lag

I have a confession: I used to believe in the wisdom of central bankers. I pictured them as sober pilots, scanning the horizon for storms, adjusting the dials with steady hands. Then I watched them miss inflation by a mile, call it transitory, and scramble like a sous-chef who forgot the sauce. Now I see them for what they are: the last guests to arrive at every party, holding a bottle of cheap wine and asking where to put their coats.

The Bank of Japan is my favorite example, mostly because it has turned delay into an art form. For decades it has been promising to normalize, to let the yield curve breathe, to stop being the market's perpetual crutch. And for decades it has found a new excuse. The BoJ is not late because it is stupid. It is late because being early is politically expensive. The moment you tighten before everyone else, you own the recession. The moment you loosen before everyone else, you own the inflation. So you wait. You wait until the data is so overwhelming that even your critics have to nod. By then, the damage is done.

## The data is a rearview mirror

Central banks love to talk about being data-dependent. That sounds rigorous. It is actually an admission of helplessness. The data they depend on is backward-looking. Employment reports tell you what happened last month. Inflation prints tell you what happened two weeks ago. GDP tells you what happened a quarter ago. By the time the data confirms a trend, the trend is already old news. It is like driving a car by watching the rearview mirror and calling yourself a careful driver.

The problem is not just the lag. It is the revision. Remember when the Fed was hiking because the labor market was tight, and then the labor market turned out to be less tight than we thought? Remember when the ECB was patting itself on the back for a soft landing, and then Germany started sneezing? The data is not a compass. It is a sketch that gets redrawn every month. And yet we treat each release like a sacred text.

I am not saying central bankers are lazy. I am saying they are trapped. Their mandate is vague, their tools are blunt, and their independence is a polite fiction. They are not masters of the universe. They are referees in a game where the rules keep changing and the players keep complaining. No wonder they wait.

## The political economy of delay

Here is the dirty secret: being late is often the safest career move. If you tighten too early and the economy slows, you are the villain who killed the recovery. If you tighten too late and inflation runs hot, you are the hero who avoided a recession. The asymmetry is brutal. Central bankers are not optimizing for the economy. They are optimizing for their own survival. And survival means never being the first to blink.

This is why the Bank of Japan has spent years in a holding pattern. Every time it hints at a move, the yen jumps, the bond market shudders, and the government whispers in its ear. The BoJ is not independent. It is a subsidiary of the Ministry of Finance with a fancy letterhead. And the Ministry of Finance does not want higher rates. Higher rates mean higher debt service. Higher debt service means less room for fiscal giveaways. So the BoJ waits. And waits. And waits.

The same story plays out everywhere. The Fed waited too long in 2021 because it did not want to be the party pooper. The ECB waited too long because it did not want to be the only one tightening. The Bank of England waited too long because it did not want to be the first to admit that Brexit was a mess. They all waited. And then they all panicked. And then they all pretended they had seen it coming.

## The illusion of forward guidance

Forward guidance was supposed to solve this. Tell the market what you are going to do, and the market will do it for you. Brilliant. Except it does not work. Because the market does not believe you. And why should it? You have changed your mind so many times that your credibility is in the toilet. You said rates would stay low until 2023. Then you said 2022. Then you said maybe sooner. Then you hiked. Then you paused. Then you hiked again. Forward guidance is not a policy tool. It is a cry for help.

The real problem is that central banks are trying to steer an economy with a joystick that is connected to a different console. They pull the lever, and something happens, but not what they expected. They push the button, and nothing happens at all. They are not pilots. They are passengers who have been given a fake steering wheel and told to look confident.

I am not saying we should abolish central banks. That would be chaos. I am saying we should stop pretending they are omniscient. They are not. They are a bunch of well-dressed people with imperfect information and a fear of being blamed. They will always be late. The only question is how late.

## What to do about it

If you are an investor, stop trying to front-run the central banks. You cannot. They do not know what they are going to do next, so how can you? Instead, position for the aftermath. When they finally move, they will move too far. They always do. The Fed will overtighten, then panic and cut. The BoJ will finally normalize, then panic and reverse. The cycle is as predictable as a sunrise.

If you are a policymaker, stop pretending you have a crystal ball. You do not. You have a rearview mirror and a lot of pressure. Admit it. Maybe then we can have a real conversation about what central banks can and cannot do. Maybe then we can stop treating them like gods and start treating them like what they are: fallible humans in a room, trying to guess the future.

And if you are a central banker, please, for the love of all that is holy, stop saying you are data-dependent. We know what that means. It means you are late. It means you are scared. It means you will wait until the last possible moment and then act like you saw it coming all along. We see you. We are not impressed.

The party is over. You missed it. Again.
